Q3241675.summary: Above the abbey church's door, Christ sits enthroned in a beaded mandorla held aloft by two angels, his right hand raised in blessing. On either side, three figures, usually read as apostles, stand beneath horseshoe arches, and a Latin inscription runs across the top of the slab. Carved almost like goldsmith's work, it is the earliest dated piece of Romanesque stone sculpture and a landmark at the very birth of the style.
facts: Its inscription records that Abbot William had it made in the twenty-fourth year of King Robert (Robert II the Pious), which corresponds to 1019–1020.
It is regarded as the oldest dated Romanesque sculpture in stone.
The horseshoe arches carved on it are thought to reflect an earlier, probably Carolingian, cloister at the abbey.

links.label: Wikipedia (fr): Linteau de l'abbaye de Saint-Génis-des-Fontaines

Q3241675.notes: The French Wikipedia article says the slab may first have served as an altar support and was set over the door only in the 12th century; the side figures are not individually identified by inscription.

cur:manuscripts-lothair-gospels-christ-i.summary: Christ, bearded and with a cross-nimbus, sits on a globe inside a tall mandorla, blessing and holding a closed book, his pale mantle falling in agitated folds. The four evangelist symbols fill the corners, and Latin verses above and below speak of the four rivers flowing from one spring — the four Gospels of the one Christ. The page is a classic Tours image of the Majestas Domini.
facts: The Gospels of Lothair was made for Emperor Lothair I at Saint-Martin de Tours in 849–851; it has 221 leaves written in gold ink and six miniatures.
Its production was overseen by one Sigilaus, and it contains the earliest depiction of Lothair, possibly the earliest monarch portrait in a biblical manuscript.

cur:manuscripts-egberti-man-born-blind.summary: Christ touches the eyes of the blind man, who leans on his staff; at the right the man appears again at the pool of Siloam, labelled 'aqueductus Siloae', where a peacock perches on the fountain.
facts: The Codex Egberti, a Gospel lectionary made for Archbishop Egbert of Trier, is described as the oldest surviving New Testament picture cycle of the life of Christ in the Ottonian era: 52 of its 60 paintings illustrate Gospel readings in the order of the church year.
Seven of its miniatures are attributed to the anonymous 'Master of the Registrum Gregorii', who worked in Trier.

cur:monumental2-bawit-room-20-christ-ent.summary: In the semidome of a niche in the east wall, Christ sits enthroned within a circular glory surrounded by the four living creatures; in the zone below, the Virgin stands at the centre among a row of apostles. This two-tier composition – Christ in glory above, Mary and the apostles on earth below – is the classic Egyptian monastic apse image, recorded here on an old glass slide soon after the excavations at Bawit.
facts: Bawit's chapels were excavated by Jean Clédat and Émile Chassinat at the beginning of the 20th century; many paintings recorded then were later lost or removed.
The slide's handwritten label reads 'Baouit. Salle 20. Niche du mur Est. Ensemble'.
cur:monumental2-bawit-room-20-christ-ent.notes: Image is a historical photograph (EuroPhot glass slide, Commons description says 'before restoration'); the painting's present location or survival was not verified.

cur:objects2-cma-ivory-pyx-miracles.summary: Carved from a section of elephant tusk, this cylindrical box is wrapped with New Testament scenes: according to the museum, the Annunciation, Christ's entry into Jerusalem, the Raising of Lazarus and the Healing of the Blind Man, together with an altar bearing chalices. The altar scene suggests that the pyx served in the liturgy, perhaps to hold the consecrated bread or relics, surrounding the Eucharist with images of Christ's life-giving power.
facts: The Greek word pyxis originally meant a box made of boxwood; the name passed to round ivory boxes of this type.
Pyxides were made from cross-sections of elephant tusk, which explains their cylindrical form.

Q116276234.summary: Set in a gold-leaf roundel on dark glass, the youthful Christ stands at the top holding out a wreath in each hand over the heads of Saints Peter and Paul, who sit facing one another below; an inscription runs around the border. Once the base of a drinking bowl, it celebrates the two great apostles of Rome receiving from Christ the crown of martyrdom.
facts: Gold-glass bowl bases like this survived in large numbers because they were pressed into the mortar of catacomb graves as markers; mortar still clings to this one.
Peter and Paul, martyred in Rome, were the most popular saints on Roman gold glass of the 4th century.
Q116276234.notes: The worklist's 'c' (place made) field was correct; set repeats Met culture/place for clarity. The inscription is not transcribed here because it was not verified letter by letter.

Q2714617.summary: Christ, robed in a blazing red garment, gazes heavenward as the crowd presses around him and an executioner prepares to strip him before the Crucifixion. In the foreground a man bores holes in the cross while the three Marys look on. El Greco's luminous figure of Christ, serene within the tumult, became one of the defining images of Spanish religious art.
facts: It was one of El Greco's first major commissions in Toledo, and a dispute over the price went to arbitration: he received only 350 ducats, though his own appraiser had valued it at 950.
Cathedral officials objected that heads in the crowd were placed above Christ's, and that the three Marys appear although the Gospels do not mention them at this moment.
The painting still hangs in the cathedral sacristy for which it was made.
